title: When the Bible’s Silence About a Woman’s Feelings Should Make Us Read More Carefully
paragraphs: When the Bible’s Silence About a Woman’s Feelings Should Make Us Read More Carefully
We have spent centuries putting words into the mouths of biblical women. Sometimes the most faithful thing we can do is stop—and listen to what Scripture actually says.
There is a woman crying at the feet of Jesus.
And almost everybody thinks they know why.
Maybe you do too.

You have heard sermons about women like her. You have seen paintings of women like her. Perhaps somewhere along the way somebody gave you an explanation for the tears before you ever noticed something unsettling about the biblical text itself:
Luke never tells us what she was feeling.
He tells us she wept.
He does not tell us exactly why.
And that difference matters more than we may realize.
Because sometimes we become so desperate to explain a person in Scripture that we accidentally replace Scripture’s silence with our imagination.
We turn possibilities into facts.
We build motives the text never gives us.
We give names to unnamed women.
We assign histories Scripture never records.
Then, after repeating those assumptions long enough, we forget which words belonged to God and which ones belonged to us.
So come inside the house with me.
But come slowly.
Leave your assumptions at the door.
A Pharisee named Simon has invited Jesus to eat with him.
Then she enters.
Luke describes her simply as “a woman in the city, which was a sinner” (Luke 7:37, KJV).
That is what Scripture gives us.
Not “prostitute.”
Not “Mary Magdalene.”
Not a detailed sexual history.
Not a psychological profile.
A woman.
A sinner.
And before we look down on her, Christianity forces an uncomfortable confession from every one of us:
So are we.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
The scandal of Luke 7 is therefore not merely that a sinful woman entered a religious man’s house.
The deeper scandal is that sinners like us can become so accustomed to categorizing somebody else’s sin that we momentarily forget our own desperate need for mercy.
She approaches Jesus carrying an alabaster vessel of ointment.
Then the tears begin.
Luke’s Greek says:
“κλαίουσα” — klaiousa.
Weeping.
The word tells us what she was doing.
It does not hand us a diary explaining every emotion moving through her heart.
That restraint should humble us.
Maybe those tears contained sorrow.
Maybe gratitude.
Maybe repentance.
Maybe relief.
Maybe several things at once.
But Scripture does not authorize us to turn any one of those possibilities into an inspired quotation from her heart.
And perhaps that is precisely where this story begins touching wounds we usually hide.
Because somebody reading this knows what it means to cry without having language strong enough to explain the crying.
You have sat alone after everyone went to sleep.
You have wiped your face before anybody noticed.
You have walked into church carrying something you could not explain to the person sitting beside you.
People saw your behavior.
God knew your heart.
People formed conclusions.
God knew the whole story.
And sometimes what hurts most is not merely what happened to you.
It is what people decided must have happened inside you.
Simon does exactly that.
He watches her touch Jesus and thinks:
“This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner.”
Notice the distance.
Simon sees a category.
Jesus sees a woman.
Simon sees contamination.
Jesus sees someone standing within reach of grace.
And then Jesus does something breathtaking.
He tells Simon a story about two debtors.
One owes five hundred denarii.
Another owes fifty.
Neither can pay.
That sentence is the Gospel hiding in a dinner conversation.
Neither.
Could.
Pay.
The size of the debts differed.
The helplessness did not.
And that is where respectable religion gets uncomfortable.
You may not have committed her sins.
She may not have committed yours.
Your past may look cleaner in public.

Your failures may have happened behind passwords, closed doors, polished reputations, church attendance, religious language, private resentment, secret pride, hidden lust, bitterness nobody detected, envy dressed as discernment, or self-righteousness disguised as holiness.
But when the debt is sin before a holy God, none of us walks to the cross carrying enough righteousness to purchase our own forgiveness.
“Neither of them had the money to pay him back.”
That is us.
Then comes grace.
The creditor forgives them.
The Greek verb behind the act in Luke 7:42 is related to charizomai—graciously giving, freely granting, forgiving.
Grace is inside the word.
The debtors do not negotiate a better payment schedule.
They do not impress the creditor into lowering the balance.
They cannot pay.
So mercy does what inability cannot.
And suddenly this unnamed woman begins looking less like somebody else's scandal and more like every Christian who has ever fallen at the feet of Christ with nothing impressive left to offer.
Jesus then turns toward her while speaking to Simon.
Do not rush past that.
He turns toward the woman.
And asks the religious man:
“Seest thou this woman?”
In Greek:
“Βλέπεις ταύτην τὴν γυναῖκα;”
Blepeis tautēn tēn gynaika?
“Do you see this woman?”
Simon had already looked at her.
But apparently looking is not always seeing.
You can look directly at someone and see only their reputation.
Their divorce.
Their addiction.
Their abortion.
Their prison record.
Their failure.
Their clothes.
Their past.
Their denomination.
Their relapse.
Their mistake.
Their scandal.
You can stare straight at a human being made in the image of God and see nothing except the label you placed over their face.
“Do you see this woman?”
That question still walks through churches.
Do you see the woman whose marriage collapsed?
Do you see the teenager hiding shame underneath rebellion?
Do you see the man who keeps showing up at church while fighting something he is terrified to confess?
Do you see the believer who fell publicly?
Do you see the person sitting quietly at the back because they are unsure whether Christians would still want them if Christians knew everything?
Do you see them?
Or do you only see what they did?
Jesus begins describing what she has done.
Simon offered no water for His feet.
She wet His feet with tears.
Simon gave Him no kiss.
She would not stop kissing His feet.
Simon did not anoint His head with oil.
She poured perfume on His feet.
And here we must be especially careful.
Jesus is not teaching that her extravagant love purchased forgiveness.
The parable immediately preceding these words establishes the direction: the debt is graciously cancelled, and the forgiven debtor responds with love.
Her love is not a bribe handed to God.
It is the fragrance of mercy received.
Grace comes first.
Love answers.
That matters because Christianity is not the announcement that broken people can perform emotionally enough to convince God to forgive them.
Christianity announces something infinitely better.
God saves sinners by grace.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until Christ can tolerate you.”
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Pay your debt.”
The Gospel says the debt you could never pay was ultimately answered by the crucified and risen Son of God.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely observe scandal from a safe distance.
He bore sin.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
The Greek New Testament later describes redemption with the language of release and forgiveness. Paul writes of Christ:
en hō echomen tēn apolytrōsin—
“in whom we have redemption.”
Christian grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
The cross proves sin mattered terribly.
Grace means Christ did for guilty people what guilty people could never accomplish for themselves.
That is why cheap grace is not the message of this woman’s tears.
And neither is self-salvation.
Jesus does not tell her, “Your perfume has saved you.”
He does not say, “Your tears have saved you.”
He does not say, “Your public humiliation has saved you.”
His final words to her are:
“Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.”
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Faith.
Saved.
Peace.
Those are the words Jesus gives us.
And perhaps we should resist our urge to improve them.
There is something profoundly beautiful about the fact that Luke does not give us a transcript of this woman’s internal monologue.
Her silence creates a boundary around our speculation.
We know what she did.
We know what Simon thought.
We know what Jesus said.
We know that her sins were many.
We know she loved much.
We know Jesus pronounced forgiveness.
We know Jesus spoke of her faith.
We know He sent her away in peace.
Everything beyond that must be held with humility.
And that principle reaches far beyond Luke 7.
Whenever Scripture does not tell us exactly what a biblical woman thought, felt, intended, or experienced, we should become more careful—not more imaginative with our certainty.
We may thoughtfully consider possibilities.
We may study historical context.
We may notice literary clues.
We may ask questions.
But there is a difference between saying, “Perhaps she felt…” and declaring, “She felt…”
That little difference protects Scripture from us.
Because even sincere Christians can accidentally make the Bible say more than the Bible says.
And there is another reason this matters.
Real women have been misunderstood this way too.
Maybe you have.
Maybe somebody interpreted your silence as arrogance when you were surviving.
Maybe they called your boundaries bitterness.
Maybe they assumed your tears meant weakness.
Maybe they saw your worst season and decided it revealed your entire identity.
Maybe people talked about you while never once talking to you.
Maybe you know the strange pain of hearing someone confidently explain your heart while getting almost everything wrong.
Then Luke 7 contains a moment you should never forget.
Jesus knows the difference between what Simon assumes and what is actually true.
He knows.
That does not mean Jesus excuses sin.
Quite the opposite.
Jesus explicitly acknowledges that the woman's sins were “many.”
Biblical grace never needs dishonesty.
Jesus can tell the complete truth about sin while refusing to reduce a sinner to sin.
That is something we desperately need to recover.
Because some people think compassion requires pretending sin is harmless.
Others think holiness requires treating sinners as hopeless.
Jesus does neither.
He calls sin what it is.
And He forgives sinners.
Truth without grace can become a weapon in human hands.
Grace without truth becomes sentimentality.
But in Jesus Christ we encounter the One John describes as “full of grace and truth.”
Maybe that is why this story feels so dangerous.
Because there are two people in the room who need Jesus.
The woman knows she needs Him.
Simon does not appear to understand the depth of his own need.
And there may be no more dangerous spiritual condition than being close enough to Jesus to host Him for dinner while remaining convinced that grace is mostly something other people need.
You can know theology and need mercy.
You can quote Scripture and need mercy.
You can preach and need mercy.
You can lead worship and need mercy.
You can expose somebody else’s sin and still desperately need mercy.
You can spend years studying the woman crying at Jesus’ feet and somehow miss that you belong beside her.
That is where this article stops being about “a woman in Luke 7.”
Now it is about you.
And me.
What are you hiding?
What memory still makes your stomach tighten when it surfaces?
What would you be terrified for your church friends to discover?
What sin have you confessed to God but secretly wondered whether the blood of Jesus could really cover?
What have you done that became a label in your own mind?
Adulterer.
Addict.
Liar.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Dirty.
Unworthy.
Ruined.
Too far gone.
Listen carefully.
Repentance does not mean pretending those sins were insignificant.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior who is greater than it.
The woman’s story is not powerful because sin was small.
It is powerful because Christ was greater.
Your hope is not that your past can be rewritten into innocence.
Your hope is that your guilt can be met by grace.
This is why the cross matters.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by changing history into fiction.
He rewrites everything by changing what sin gets to say about the future of the person who belongs to Him.
Guilty can become forgiven.
Far away can be brought near.
Lost can be found.
Condemned sinners can be justified through faith in Christ.
Enemies can be reconciled.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
Scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Maybe you entered this article identifying with the woman.
Before you leave, consider whether you might also resemble Simon.
Have you turned someone’s worst chapter into their permanent name?
Have you confidently assigned motives God never revealed to you?
Have you repeated something about a biblical woman—or a real woman—because you heard it so many times that you never stopped to ask whether it was actually true?
Have you been better at detecting another person's scandal than remembering your own need for grace?
Repentance belongs here too.
Because the Gospel humbles the disgraced sinner and the respectable sinner at the same cross.
Neither can pay.
Both need grace.
That is the breathtaking equality of Calvary.
Nobody gets to boast.
And nobody who comes to Christ in genuine faith and repentance needs to believe that their sin is stronger than His saving grace.
So maybe the next time you encounter an unnamed woman in Scripture, resist the temptation to fill every silence.
Read slower.
Ask what the text actually says.
Ask what it does not say.
Distinguish interpretation from revelation.
Let Scripture speak with its own voice.
And when you encounter a wounded person in real life, remember Jesus’ question:
“Do you see this woman?”
Not the rumor.
Not the category.
Not the scandal.
The woman.
The person.
The soul.
And if you are the one carrying the scandal tonight, look again at Jesus.
The deepest message of Luke 7 is not that an unnamed woman cried beautifully.
It is that Jesus Christ has authority to forgive sinners.
The people at the table understood how enormous that claim was.
“Who is this that forgiveth sins also?”
Exactly.
That is the question.
Who is this Jesus?
Christianity rises or falls there.
He is not merely someone who makes wounded people feel better about themselves.
He is the Savior.
The Son of God.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One before whom repentance is possible because mercy is real.
The One who does not need Simon’s assumptions to know the woman completely.
The One who does not need your carefully edited testimony to know you completely either.
He already knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop negotiating with the debt you cannot pay.
Stop trying to manufacture enough righteousness to erase yesterday.
Stop letting shame preach a counterfeit gospel in which Jesus can rescue everybody except you.
Bring the truth into the light.
Bring the sin.
Bring the regret.
Bring the questions.
Bring the tears you cannot explain.
Come to Christ.

And if grace has already met you in places you thought were beyond restoration, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you glorify God.
It does not.
Christ purchased salvation; we cannot purchase His approval.
Supporting Gospel work should flow from grace and willing generosity—not guilt, spiritual pressure, or an attempt to buy blessing.
Jesus.
Not the platform.
Not the merchandise.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Jesus Christ.
Because one day every page will disappear.
Every social platform will become history.
Every book will close.
Every human ministry will end.
But Christ remains.
So share the truth.
Support faithful Gospel work where God leads you.
Read Scripture carefully.
Refuse to build accusations where God left silence.
Repent when you sin.
Forgive as one who has been forgiven.
And never forget the woman whose feelings Scripture did not completely explain—but whose Savior Scripture revealed unmistakably.
She entered the story known by her sin.
She left hearing words about faith, salvation, and peace.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you:
When Jesus has spoken grace over the repentant sinner, shame does not get to write the ending.
